The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study, run by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation
(IHME), estimates how many deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in every country and
year since 1990 are attributable to occupational risks: carcinogens, asthmagens, particulate
matter, gases and fumes, noise, injuries, and ergonomic factors. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**Before you start:** this notebook needs data you download yourself from IHME. Follow
"Getting the data" in the README, then run `scripts/prepare_data.R`.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

path <- file.path("..", "data", "processed", "gbd_occupational.csv.gz")
if (!file.exists(path)) {
  stop("No prepared GBD data. Download the data as described in the README, put the files in ",
       "data/raw/, and run scripts/prepare_data.R.")
}
gbd <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)

latest <- max(gbd$year)
cat("Years", min(gbd$year), "to", latest, "\n")
count(distinct(gbd, level, location), level)

# The six occupational risks one level below "Occupational risks"
level3 <- c("Occupational carcinogens", "Occupational asthmagens",
            "Occupational particulate matter, gases, and fumes", "Occupational noise",
            "Occupational injuries", "Occupational ergonomic factors")
```

The **metric** matters:

- `Number`: deaths or DALYs.
- `Rate`: per 100,000 people (the whole population, not only workers).
- `Percent`: share of **all** deaths or DALYs from every cause (stored as a proportion, so 0.02
  means 2%).

Every estimate has a 95% uncertainty interval (`lower` to `upper`).

# Part 1. The global burden over time

```{r global}
global <- gbd |>
  filter(location == "Global", risk == "Occupational risks", sex == "Both")

global |>
  filter(metric == "Number", age == "All ages") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, val / 1e6, ymin = lower / 1e6, ymax = upper / 1e6)) +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Burden attributable to occupational risks, world", x = NULL, y = "Millions")

global |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, latest), age %in% c("All ages", "Age-standardized")) |>
  mutate(value = case_when(metric == "Number" ~ round(val),
                           metric == "Percent" ~ round(val * 100, 2),
                           TRUE ~ round(val, 1))) |>
  select(measure, metric, age, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. About how many deaths and DALYs were attributable to occupational risks in the latest year?
   What share of all deaths is that?
2. Compare the trend in the *number* of deaths with the trend in the *age-standardized rate*. Why
   might they move differently? (Think about population growth and ageing.)
3. Why do DALYs tell a different story from deaths for some risks (hint: think about back pain
   and hearing loss)?

# Part 2. Which occupational risks matter most?

```{r risks}
by_risk <- gbd |>
  filter(location == "Global", sex == "Both", age == "All ages", metric == "Number",
         year == latest, risk %in% level3)

ggplot(by_risk, aes(val, fct_reorder(risk, val), xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_linerange() +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = paste("Burden by occupational risk, world,", latest), x = NULL, y = NULL)

# The 13 carcinogens
gbd |>
  filter(location == "Global", sex == "Both", age == "All ages", metric == "Number",
         measure == "Deaths", year == latest, str_starts(risk, "Occupational exposure to")) |>
  mutate(risk = str_remove(risk, "Occupational exposure to "), deaths = round(val)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths)) |>
  select(risk, deaths, lower, upper)
```

**Questions**

1. Which occupational risk causes the most deaths? Which causes the most DALYs? Why are they
   different?
2. Which carcinogen causes the most deaths? Many countries banned it decades ago. Why does it still
   cause so many deaths?
3. Injuries are what most national OSH statistics count. What share of the occupational burden do
   injuries make up in GBD?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Regions

Age-standardized rates take out differences in the age structure of populations, so regions can
be compared fairly.

```{r regions}
regions <- gbd |>
  filter(level == "Region", risk == "Occupational risks", sex == "Both",
         age == "Age-standardized", metric == "Rate", measure == "DALYs")

regions |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, latest)) |>
  select(location, year, val) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = val, names_prefix = "y") |>
  mutate(change = round(100 * (.data[[paste0("y", latest)]] / y1990 - 1))) |>
  arrange(desc(.data[[paste0("y", latest)]]))

ggplot(regions, aes(year, val, group = location)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = filter(regions, location %in% c("High-income North America", "South Asia",
                                                   "Western Sub-Saharan Africa", "East Asia")),
            aes(colour = location)) +
  labs(title = "Age-standardized DALY rate from occupational risks", x = NULL,
       y = "DALYs per 100,000", colour = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which regions have the highest and lowest age-standardized DALY rates? Has the gap between
   them grown or shrunk since 1990?
2. Suggest two reasons why the burden differs so much between regions (think about the kinds of
   work people do, and about regulation).
3. The rate is per 100,000 *people*, not per 100,000 *workers*. How could that affect comparisons
   between regions with different shares of people in work?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Countries

```{r countries}
countries <- gbd |>
  filter(level == "Country", risk == "Occupational risks", sex == "Both",
         age == "Age-standardized", metric == "Rate")

countries |>
  filter(year == latest, measure == "DALYs") |>
  arrange(desc(val)) |>
  select(location, val, lower, upper) |>
  slice(c(1:10, (n() - 9):n()))

# Countries with modules in this repository
compare <- c("United States of America", "Canada", "United Kingdom", "Australia")
countries |>
  filter(location %in% compare, year %in% c(1990, latest)) |>
  mutate(val = round(val, 1)) |>
  select(location, measure, year, val) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = val)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries have the highest and lowest rates? Look at the uncertainty intervals: are the
   top countries clearly different from each other?
2. Compare the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and Australia. How do their rates and
   trends compare? Does this match what you saw in those countries' injury statistics (CFOI,
   AWCBC, RIDDOR, Safe Work Australia modules)?
3. Find a country you are interested in. What drives its occupational burden (repeat the Part 2
   breakdown for that country, using the country file's six risks)?

# Part 5. Occupational risks in context

```{r context}
gbd |>
  filter(location == "Global", sex != "Both", age == "Age-standardized", metric == "Rate",
         measure == "DALYs", risk %in% level3, year == latest) |>
  select(risk, sex, val) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = val) |>
  mutate(male_to_female = round(Male / Female, 1))

gbd |>
  filter(location == "Global", sex == "Both", age == "All ages", metric == "Percent",
         risk == "Occupational risks", year == latest) |>
  mutate(percent = round(val * 100, 2), lower = round(lower * 100, 2),
         upper = round(upper * 100, 2)) |>
  select(measure, percent, lower, upper)
```

**Questions**

1. For which risks is the burden in men much higher than in women? Are any higher in women? Why?
2. About what percent of all DALYs worldwide are attributable to occupational risks? For
   comparison, GBD attributes far more to tobacco or to high blood pressure. Does
   that mean occupational health is a small problem? (Think about who bears the burden, and
   whether it is preventable.)
3. GBD's list of occupational risks leaves out long working hours, shift work, job strain and many
   chemicals. Which of these do you think would add the most, and why?
